A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hot-boning of beef is a good way to increase the functionality of meat, especially when the meat is used for processing.
the effect of hot-bone processing is muscle-dependent and the effect of reducing phosphate level is more pronounced in the muscle with the lower functionality.
the effect of boning method and phosphate level on functionality of beef is dependent upon the muscle type.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of hot-boning to increase meat functionality in low-value muscles, such as IS and PP, is not as beneficial as in the case of higher value muscles, such as M. semimembranosus, and that reducing the amount of phosphate in brine during processing can lead to products with inferior sensory and processing properties.
the effects of hot-boning are not uniform throughout the carcass and that the effects of reduced phosphate levels in brines are not consistent.
hot-boning of forequarter muscles is feasible, however, the effect on processing and sensory attributes of the product is variable depending on muscle type.
